Basal metabolic rate in Speke (Gazella spekei) was assessed through respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions; at a core body temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C], the maximum recorded oxygen consumption reached 5926 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 5926 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This substantial metabolic rate, measured in post-absorptive adults resting within their thermoneutral zone, aligns with the relatively high energetic demands expected for a medium-sized ungulate inhabiting semi-arid landscapes. The value exceeds what has been reported for the closely related Dorcas gazelle (Gazella dorcas), suggesting that Speke may sustain a more elevated metabolic throughput, possibly as an adaptation to the unpredictable resource pulses characteristic of the Horn of Africa. Comparative analyses of ruminant energetics indicate that such a metabolic profile often correlates with a high-quality diet and a correspondingly rapid processing of forage, both of which facilitate the maintenance of a large home range while meeting the physiological costs of thermoregulation and locomotion.

Female Speke gazelles ultimately attain a maximum adult body mass of 20,000 grams [Wwi = 20,000 grams], a value that serves as the asymptotic endpoint of their growth trajectory. This body size is moderate among the gazelle assemblage, positioning them between the smaller G. dorcas and the larger G. granti. The postnatal growth pattern involves a prolonged period of skeletal and muscular development, with individuals approaching their final mass only after several years. In contrast, neonates enter the world at a considerably smaller scale: the wet weight at birth is 1253 grams [Wwb = 1253 grams], a relatively altricial starting point that nonetheless represents a substantial investment by the mother given her own body size. The ratio of birth weight to adult female mass approximates six percent, a figure consistent with the precocial developmental mode observed across the antilopinae, wherein newborn calves are sufficiently developed to follow the herd within hours of parturition.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a modest litter size and a prolonged interval between successive births. Females typically produce a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter], a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over numerical quantity. The interval between consecutive litters averages 205 days [F_R_i = averages 205 days], measured under the standard metabolic temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C] that approximates the species core body temperature. This inter-birth period is relatively extended compared to smaller-bodied gazelles, reflecting the demands placed on the maternal energy budget by gestation and lactation. Gestation itself, for female calves, lasts 197 days [tg = 197 days] at this same body temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C], a duration that is intermediate among the gazellini and allows for substantial foetal development prior to the energetically costly birth event. The maximum reproduction rate at this temperature reaches 1 calf per 205 days [Ri = 1 calf per 205 days], reflecting the combined effect of litter size and inter-birth interval.

The time since birth at puberty for females is 711 days [tp = 711 days], again at 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C], meaning that reproductive maturity is typically attained at around two years of age. This relatively delayed onset of sexual maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes reaching a sufficient body size before committing resources to gestation and lactation, thereby improving the likelihood of successful first reproduction.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 5110 days [am = 5110 days], corresponding to approximately fourteen years, when evaluated at the standard core body temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that reported for other medium-sized gazelles in captivity, although wild individuals likely experience reduced survival due to predation, disease, and nutritional stress. The relationship between body size and lifespan across the Bovidae suggests that Speke gazelles live near the predicted duration given their 20,000 gram [Wwi = 20,000 gram] adult mass. Physiological senescence in older individuals manifests as declining tooth wear, reduced mobility, and diminished reproductive output, with females typically ceasing ovulation several years before the terminal age. Field observations from the Somali region confirm that the oldest documented free-ranging individuals rarely exceed a decade, underscoring the challenges of reaching the species full physiological potential in a semi-arid environment.
